findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The method `_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is dead code: no call site anywhere in the diff or existing code invokes it, and its restart path is superseded by `_create_process_for_shards` called directly from `_ensure_processes_alive`. Next reader assumes single-shard restart granularity exists and wires new logic to it; it silently diverges from the real per-process-group restart path and will be deleted or misused later.

[ADVISORY] The metric tag key is inconsistent: `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses tag key `shards` while `produce` and `segment_size_bytes` on adjacent lines use `shard`, and the flusher_unhealthy metric uses `shard` with an int value while these use a comma-joined string. Whoever builds dashboards for this PR gets two parallel tag series for the same dimension and mixed tag value formats (string vs int) across metrics, splitting alerts on flusher health by shard across incompatible tag keys.

[ADVISORY] In `join`, `remaining_time` is computed into a local variable and only used for the `<= 0` check; the value is never passed to any wait, making it dead computation that misleads the reader into thinking the remaining budget is honored per-process. A future maintainer changing the join timeout logic will assume per-process budget accounting exists when the loop actually only re-checks the global deadline, making the next change to shutdown behavior riskier than it looks.

[ADVISORY] In `submit`, the backpressure branch increments `spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure` and raises `MessageRejected` inside the loop over `process_backpressure_since`, so the metric fires once per backpressured process per submit call instead of once per submit as before. Operators comparing backpressure metric rates before and after this deploy see inflated counts proportional to the number of stalled flusher processes, breaking alert thresholds tuned on the old semantics.

[ADVISORY] `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` mean `--flusher-processes 0` (a plausible fat-fingered deploy value, since the click option is an unvalidated int with default 1) is silently coerced to one process per shard, i.e. the maximum rather than the minimum. An operator setting the new `--flusher-processes 0` flag expecting to disable extra flushers instead spawns one process per shard, multiplying Redis connections and memory beyond what the deploy was sized for.

[BUG] The restart path never kills hung processes when produce_to_pipe is set (threading.Thread mode), so a hung flusher thread keeps running while a second thread for the same shards is started, producing duplicate segments. In pipe/test mode, a 'hang'-detected flusher thread is not terminated (the kill is skipped for non-multiprocessing.Process objects), so after restart two threads poll the same Redis shards and each flushes the same segments, double-emitting spans to Kafka/the pipe.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten health/restart logic (_ensure_processes_alive: per-process hang detection, MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS RuntimeError, per-process backpressure-driven MessageRejected) has no test anywhere in the diff. Neither test_consumer.py nor test_flusher.py exercises process-crash restart, the repeated-restart RuntimeError, or per-process backpressure rejection; a regression in restart bookkeeping (e.g. process_restarts never reset, or the wrong process_index restarted) would ship unverified.

[ADVISORY] Metric tags are inconsistent: 'spans.buffer.flusher.produce' and 'segment_size_bytes' use tags={"shard": ...} while 'wait_produce' uses tags={"shards": ...} for the same shard_tag value. Anyone building dashboards/alerts on flusher metrics gets wait_produce split into a separate 'shards' tag dimension from the other two metrics, silently fragmenting the time series per shard.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code: no caller exists in this diff or in the factory. The method restarts a whole process to recover one shard and is never invoked; the next maintainer must guess whether restarts go through it or through _create_process_for_shards, adding a second divergent restart entry point to keep in sync.

[ADVISORY] The fix for the multiprocess timing race is a bare time.sleep(0.1) rather than a deterministic synchronization on flush completion. Under CI load the 0.1s window can elapse before flusher threads process the drifted clock, intermittently failing the test's message assertions for whoever touches this file next.

[ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit verifies process count and shard distribution but never submits a message, so the actual end-to-end flush behavior under process sharing is unverified. A bug where two processes both claim the same shard (or a shard is dropped from every process's buffer) passes this test because no data flows through the 2-process/4-shard topology before step.join().

[ADVISORY] The diff adds an unrelated Python style rule about hasattr() vs isinstance() to CLAUDE.md, which has no connection to the stated PR intent of span buffer multiprocess enhancement and health monitoring. Reviewers and future archaeologists tracing this PR cannot attribute this doc change to any requirement; it silently rides along and pollutes the commit's scope, and if the PR is reverted the style guidance is lost or inconsistently reverted with it.

[BUG] _create_process_for_shard() is dead code — no call site anywhere in the diff; the restart loop in _ensure_processes_alive invokes _create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards) directly, so the shard-lookup helper is unreachable. The next maintainer editing the restart path may modify the wrong helper (the shard-keyed one) and see no effect, or the duplicated restart entry points drift apart; it also misleads readers into thinking restarts are keyed by shard when they are keyed by process index.

[ADVISORY] Metric tag keys are inconsistent across the new instrumentation: 'spans.buffer.flusher.produce' and 'spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes' use tag {"shard": shard_tag} while 'spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce' uses tag {"shards": shard_tag}, and the flusher_unhealthy counter tags an int shard while the timers tag a joined string. Anyone building dashboards/alerts on flusher metrics must handle two tag names plus two value formats for the same concept, and any tag-based aggregation in Sentry's metrics pipeline will split the series, making the health monitoring this PR is named for harder to actually observe.

[ADVISORY] The Redis memory check in submit() now calls get_memory_info() once per per-shard SpansBuffer (N remote calls where the code previously made one), and record_stored_segments() is likewise invoked once per buffer per submit, because each restart-safe process gets its own freshly constructed SpansBuffer wrapping the same Redis backend. On a consumer with many shards and max-memory-percentage < 1.0, every submit (which the code itself notes can run many times per second) performs N Redis/service info round-trips instead of one, a hot-path regression in exactly the configuration used when operators are already worried about memory.

[ADVISORY] The backpressure metric in submit() is incremented once per unhealthy process inside the loop, so a single submit with two backpressured processes emits two 'spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure' increments, and it fires on every submit for the entire backpressure window rather than once at the threshold crossing as the previous single-process code did. Operators watching the backpressure counter see inflated, process-count-multiplied counts that cannot be compared to pre-deploy baselines, defeating the monitoring goal of the PR.

[ADVISORY] The multi-process health/restart path (_ensure_processes_alive with a dead or hung process among several, MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS exhaustion raising RuntimeError naming the shard set, and per-process healthy_since reset on restart) has no test coverage in this diff — test_consumer.py only asserts process-count and shard-mapping invariants, and test_flusher.py only checks a backpressure flag. A regression in per-process restart logic (e.g. killing the wrong process, losing a shard's flusher permanently because a restarted process map entry is stale) would ship silently; the core health-monitoring behavior the PR title advertises is exercised only on the happy path.

[ADVISORY] The SpanFlusher no longer stores or uses the consumer's original buffer (self.buffer = buffer was deleted), instead constructing N fresh SpansBuffer(shards) objects whose only relationship to the parent is the shard list; whether these buffers preserve any parent-level state or configuration is invisible in this diff and unverified by any test that constructs buffers with differing state. If SpansBuffer carries configuration beyond the shard list (e.g. Redis namespace, TTL, or options read at construction), the per-shard buffers silently diverge from the buffer the rest of the consumer writes through, and segments written via the parent path would never be flushed by the per-shard flushers.

[BUG] The `wait_produce` metrics timer uses tag key "shards" while the `produce` and `segment_size_bytes` timers on the same code path use tag key "shard", so the two metric series cannot be joined/grouped together. Dashboards and alerts that aggregate flusher timing by shard will silently split wait_produce into a separate dimension; anyone correlating produce latency with wait latency per shard gets empty series for one of the two.

[ADVISORY] submit() now calls `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()` once per buffer object (one per flusher process) instead of once per consumer, multiplying the Redis round trips per submit by the number of flusher processes. On every submitted message the consumer issues N Redis calls where it previously issued 1; with flusher_processes scaled to shard count on a high-throughput topic this is a measurable hot-path latency and Redis load regression, plus the stored-segments metric is recorded N times per submit (counter inflation) since every buffer instance reports the same segments.

[ADVISORY] `_create_process_for_shard` is dead code in this diff (no caller) and, unlike `_ensure_processes_alive`, restarts a process without consulting `process_restarts` or MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS. Any future caller of this convenience method silently bypasses the crash-loop protection that the monitored restart path enforces, restarting a crash-looping process forever instead of raising RuntimeError to restart the consumer.

[ADVISORY] join() `break`s out of the whole for-loop once the deadline is exhausted, so processes later in the dict never reach their `terminate()` call. During a shutdown that times out, some flusher processes are left un-terminated (relying solely on daemon=True to reap them), and any non-daemon cleanup those processes needed is skipped — shutdown behavior now depends on dict iteration order.

[ADVISORY] The memory backpressure check sums `used` and `available` across N ServiceMemory results that each report the same host's memory (one SpansBuffer per flusher process), inflating both sides by a factor of N. If ServiceMemory is host-level (Redis memory info), the used/available ratio is computed from duplicated samples; per-host granularity is lost and the threshold decision becomes an average over identical values rather than a per-shard or per-host check, masking a single hot shard's memory pressure when buffers report the same host.

[ADVISORY] `SpanFlusher.main` is a public static method whose signature gained a required `shards` positional parameter, with only the in-diff call site updated. Any out-of-tree or not-updated caller invoking SpanFlusher.main with the old arity (buffer, stopped, ...) now passes `stopped` as `shards` and shifts every subsequent argument, failing confusingly rather than with a clear contract error; the changed public surface carries no versioning note.

[ADVISORY] The backpressure MessageRejected check now iterates all per-process `backpressure_since` values but increments the `spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure` metric inside the loop, once per offending process per submit call. On a consumer with several flusher processes in backpressure, the backpressure metric fires N times per submitted message, inflating the counter by N× and distorting any alerting/aggregation keyed on that metric's rate.

[BUG] The default value of max_processes=None silently changes the flusher from one process handling all shards to one process per shard for every caller that does not pass flusher_processes. ProcessSpansStrategyFactory defaults flusher_processes=None (factory.py line 41), so any deployment or test constructing the factory without the new click option spawns len(assigned_shards) processes per consumer instead of the previous single process — a memory/COGS and process-count behavioral change to the existing span-buffer deployment made without any explicit operator opt-in, changing the accepted prior behavior.

[BUG] join() breaks out of the process loop when the deadline expires, skipping terminate() for all remaining processes in the dict. On a slow shutdown with multiple flusher processes, if the deadline is hit while waiting on process 0, the `break` exits the for-loop and processes 1..N-1 are never waited on nor terminated, leaking spawned child processes that hold Redis connections and the stopped flag — the original code guaranteed terminate() on the single process, so the shutdown contract this component had is silently violated.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard is dead code — no call site exists anywhere in the diff. The next maintainer extending restart logic has two near-identical restart paths (per-shard vs per-index) to reason about; the per-shard variant also has an inconsistent semantic (restart only one process for a shard but via a linear scan). Deletion removes the method and the ambiguity.

[BUG] The test's `time.sleep(0.1)` intended to give flusher threads time is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep globally to `lambda _: None` at the top of the function. test_basic's newly added synchronization wait does nothing, so the test passes (or flakes) without the threads having processed the drift change — the comment states an intent the code does not achieve, and a future reader will trust a wait that never happens.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten backpressure assertion `assert any(x.value for x in flusher.process_backpressure_since.values())` weakens the original `assert flusher.backpressure_since.value` from asserting the specific monitored value to asserting at least one of N values is truthy. A regression where backpressure detection is broken on most processes but sporadically set on one will pass the test; the original test's guarantee that the flusher under test actually observed backpressure is silently reduced by the rewrite.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds an unrelated isinstance-vs-hasattr Python style example to CLAUDE.md in a PR titled 'Span Buffer Multiprocess Enhancement with Health Monitoring'. Unrelated documentation drift mixed into a behavioral PR obscures review provenance and pollutes the commit history of both concerns; anyone bisecting style-guide changes or reverting the flusher change gets entangled with the other.

[ADVISORY] submit() now calls buffer.record_stored_segments() once per per-shard SpansBuffer instead of once on the original single buffer, and get_memory_info() is likewise spread across N buffers, changing what those metrics report relative to the pre-PR single-buffer semantics. Any consumer of spans.buffer stored-segment metrics or memory-based backpressure now sees behavior aggregated over N fresh SpansBuffer instances created inside the flusher rather than the factory's buffer the consumer writes through; if SpansBuffer tracks in-process state (not purely Redis-keyed), the health/memory monitoring numbers silently diverge from what the original design's shared buffer measured.

[BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` 'give flusher threads time' wait in test_basic is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at its top, so the synchronization the comment promises never happens. The two extra `step.poll()` calls and the sleep were added to make the multiprocess flusher deterministic, but the sleep is patched out by the test's own monkeypatch, so the test passes (or flakes) without actually waiting for the new background threads — any race the wait was meant to eliminate is still live, and the diff's only coverage of the multi-shard flush path in test_basic is timing-luck.

[ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit is a mirror test that asserts only the flusher's internal data structures (len(flusher.processes), max_processes, num_processes, process_to_shards_map contents) and never submits a message or asserts any span is flushed, so it verifies the implementation's bookkeeping, not the behavior. If the shard→process mapping produced a misconfigured SpansBuffer (e.g. a process reading shards whose segments are actually written under different Redis keys), or if the 2-process flusher dropped every segment, this test still passes; the data-flow through multiple flusher processes — the actual feature of this PR — is exercised by no test in the diff (test_consumer.py was checked: test_basic still uses one partition; test_flusher.py was checked: it only touches backpressure state).

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code — no call site exists anywhere in the diff (restarts go through _create_process_for_shards plural in _ensure_processes_alive), and no test references it. The next maintainer adding a single-shard restart path will 'use' this never-executed, never-tested helper and inherit whatever drift it accumulates against the real restart path; it should be deleted. Checked test_consumer.py and test_flusher.py — neither calls it.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten per-process health/restart logic in _ensure_processes_alive (hang detection via process_healthy_since, kill, restart-count check raising RuntimeError, per-shard unhealthy metrics) has zero test coverage in this diff — test_flusher.py was checked and only asserts backpressure state; test_consumer.py was checked and covers only the happy path. A regression in the restart path (e.g. the new `if not process: continue` guard, the moved `self.process_restarts[process_index] += 1` increment after the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS comparison, or the isinstance-guarded kill leaving a zombie Thread alive while a new one is spawned) ships unverified; in production this code decides whether the whole consumer restarts, so a wrong branch means either infinite zombie respawn or spurious RuntimeError consumer crashes.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten multi-process join() (per-process deadline slicing, terminate on each process) has no test — test_flusher.py and test_consumer.py in this diff both end with a bare step.join()/flusher join with no assertion that all processes terminated or that timeout semantics hold. The deadline arithmetic (`remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the whole for-loop, skipping terminate() for the remaining processes) is untested; if it's wrong, consumer shutdown leaves spawned flusher processes un-terminated and the consumer hangs on deploy/restart.

[BUG] Default behavior silently changes from one flusher process total to one process per shard: with max_processes=None (the factory default when --flusher-processes is not passed), self.max_processes falls back to len(buffer.assigned_shards), spawning N processes each constructing its own SpansBuffer with its own Redis connections and Kafka producer. A consumer with e.g. 32 assigned shards goes from 1 flusher process to 32 on deploy with no config change, multiplying Redis connections and spawned processes by shard count; the CLI flag defaults to 1 only for the ingest-spans consumer, so any other construction path (or an operator omitting the flag) gets the shard-per-process explosion and potential resource exhaustion/COGS spike, with no backfill of the intended '1 process' behavior.

[ADVISORY] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() on the flusher's fresh per-shard SpansBuffer instances (self.buffers) instead of the shared buffer the consumer's write path uses, so the original buffer passed to the flusher constructor never has record_stored_segments called on it in the parent process. If record_stored_segments carries any local/in-memory state on the buffer object (as opposed to a per-shard Redis write), the writer-side backpressure accounting that previously updated the shared buffer now updates orphaned copies, and backpressure detection silently degrades; anyone relying on the flusher honoring insertion-pause signals gets unbounded Redis growth instead.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code — nothing in the diff or existing callers invokes it, and its behavior (restart by shard) is duplicated by the loop in _ensure_processes_alive calling _create_process_for_shards directly. The next person changing restart logic has two near-identical methods to reason about and may edit the dead one believing it runs; delete it.

[ADVISORY] Metric tags are inconsistent across the same code path: the produce/segment-size timers use tag key "shard" with a comma-joined list while wait_produce uses key "shards", so dashboards aggregating by shard tag split the same process's metrics into two cardinality streams. Anyone building flusher health dashboards per shard sees produce timings and wait_produce timings under different tag keys with different value formats (single int vs "0,2,3"), silently breaking aggregation.

[ADVISORY] The memory-pressure check in submit() now calls get_memory_info() on every per-shard-group SpansBuffer on every message, multiplying the remote/Redis memory-info calls by process count on the hot path. In the default configuration (max_processes=None -> one process per assigned shard), each consumed message now triggers N memory-info lookups instead of one; operators with many partitions see an N-fold increase in Redis round-trips and CPU on the consumer's submit path, degrading throughput exactly when the consumer is busiest.

[ADVISORY] In _ensure_processes_alive(), a crashed flusher process is kill()ed and replaced but never join()ed or waited on, so the killed SpawnProcess becomes a zombie until the replaced object is garbage-collected. Under a crash-looping flusher (e.g., Redis outage causing repeated exits), each restart cycle leaks a zombie process entry; the container accumulates zombies and can eventually hit the process limit, taking down the whole consumer even though the restart logic believes it is recovering.

[ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard() restarts a shard's process by creating a new one for the same process_index without killing or stopping the existing process first, so two processes would run concurrently for the same shards. Any future caller of this method (it is currently dead code — nothing in the diff invokes it) silently double-runs flushes for the same shards, producing duplicate Kafka production and racing on the shared backpressure/healthy Values; as written it is a latent trap for the next contributor who wires it up.

[ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats an explicitly configured value of 0 as falsy, silently falling back to one process per shard. An operator who sets --flusher-processes 0 intending to disable extra flusher processes gets the maximum process count instead, spawning one process per shard with no error or warning — the opposite of the requested configuration.

[ADVISORY] The produce and wait_produce timers use inconsistent tag keys ("shard" vs "shards") with a comma-joined shard-list value that changes on every partition rebalance or restart reassignment. Anyone building dashboards or alerts on spans.buffer.flusher.produce by shard gets two disjoint tag namespaces for the same logical dimension, and the comma-joined values churn as assignments change, fragmenting the metric series and making per-shard alerting unreliable.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.join`, the loop computes `remaining_time = deadline - time.time()` but never uses it to bound any wait/join call; the actual waiting condition is `while process.is_alive() and (deadline is None or deadline > time.time())`. So the variable only gates an early `break` and does not provide per-process timeout budgeting, which can mislead maintainers into thinking remaining budget is being applied to a specific wait operation.

The code then overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` with the new thread, losing the reference to the old one, which can keep running/resume later and flush the same Redis shards, causing duplicate emissions.

On every submitted message the consumer issues N Redis calls where it previously issued 1; with flusher_processes scaled to shard count on a high-throughput topic this is a measurable hot-path latency and Redis load regression, plus the stored-segments metric is recorded N times per submit (counter inflation) since every buffer instance reports the same segments.

However, the finding’s claim of stored-segments metric “counter inflation” because each buffer reports the same segments is not verifiable from the diff: each buffer is constructed with different shard subsets (`SpansBuffer(shards)`), so they may report disjoint data rather than duplicates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The memory backpressure check sums `used` and `available` across N ServiceMemory results that each report the same host's memory (one SpansBuffer per flusher process), inflating both sides by a factor of N. If ServiceMemory is host-level (Redis memory info), the used/available ratio is computed from duplicated samples; per-host granularity is lost and the threshold decision becomes an average over identical values rather than a per-shard or per-host check, masking a single hot shard's memory pressure when buffers report the same host.

This is a real, diff-grounded design/monitoring concern, but not a clearly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.

On a slow shutdown with multiple flusher processes, if the deadline is hit while waiting on process 0, the `break` exits the for-loop and processes 1..N-1 are never waited on nor terminated, leaking spawned child processes that hold Redis connections and the stopped flag — the original code guaranteed terminate() on the single process, so the shutdown contract this component had is silently violated.

If shutdown is slow and the deadline is exceeded while handling an earlier process, remaining processes can be left running, which is a behavior regression versus the prior single-process implementation that always hit `terminate()` for that process.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] submit() now calls buffer.record_stored_segments() once per per-shard SpansBuffer instead of once on the original single buffer, and get_memory_info() is likewise spread across N buffers, changing what those metrics report relative to the pre-PR single-buffer semantics. Any consumer of spans.buffer stored-segment metrics or memory-based backpressure now sees behavior aggregated over N fresh SpansBuffer instances created inside the flusher rather than the factory's buffer the consumer writes through; if SpansBuffer tracks in-process state (not purely Redis-keyed), the health/memory monitoring numbers silently diverge from what the original design's shared buffer measured.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does change monitoring/backpressure inputs from a single shared `SpansBuffer` to multiple per-process `SpansBuffer` instances created inside `SpanFlusher` (`shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)` in `_create_process_for_shards`). In `submit()`, `record_stored_segments()` is now invoked for each buffer in `self.buffers.values()` (previously a single call), and `get_memory_info()` is now aggregated by extending `memory_infos` from each buffer (previously only `self.buffer.get_memory_info()`). This is a real, diff-grounded semantics change that could affect how stored-segment metrics and memory-based backpressure are reported/triggered, but whether it is a correctness defect depends on `SpansBuffer` internals which are not shown here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` 'give flusher threads time' wait in test_basic is a no-op because the same test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at its top, so the synchronization the comment promises never happens. adjudication.rationale: In `test_basic`, the test monkeypatches `time.sleep` at the top (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), and later the diff adds `time.sleep(0.1)` with a comment saying it gives flusher threads time to process. Given the monkeypatch, that new sleep is a no-op and cannot provide the intended synchronization, so any race it was meant to mitigate remains unaddressed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_flusher_processes_limit is a mirror test that asserts only the flusher's internal data structures (len(flusher.processes), max_processes, num_processes, process_to_shards_map contents) and never submits a message or asserts any span is flushed, so it verifies the implementation's bookkeeping, not the behavior. If the shard→process mapping produced a misconfigured SpansBuffer (e.g. a process reading shards whose segments are actually written under different Redis keys), or if the 2-process flusher dropped every segment, this test still passes; the data-flow through multiple flusher processes — the actual feature of this PR — is exercised by no test in the diff (test_consumer.py was checked: test_basic still uses one partition; test_flusher.py was checked: it only touches backpressure state).

adjudication.rationale: In the added test `test_flusher_processes_limit` (tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_consumer.py), the assertions only inspect `fac._flusher` internals (`len(flusher.processes)`, `flusher.max_processes`, `flusher.num_processes`, and `process_to_shards_map` shard counts). The test never calls `step.submit(...)`, never causes segments to be written/flushed, and never asserts any `KafkaPayload` was produced. Meanwhile, the other modified tests don’t exercise multi-shard/multi-process flushing behavior either (`test_basic` still uses one partition; test_flusher only checks backpressure state). So the finding that the core data-flow behavior of the new multi-process shard handling is not covered by a behavior-level test is diff-grounded and actionable, but not itself a correctness defect proven by the diff.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/flusher.py`, `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is newly added but has no call sites in the shown diff: initialization uses `_create_processes()` / `_create_process_for_shards()`, and restarts in `_ensure_processes_alive()` also call `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The rewritten per-process health/restart logic in _ensure_processes_alive (hang detection via process_healthy_since, kill, restart-count check raising RuntimeError, per-shard unhealthy metrics) has zero test coverage in this diff — test_flusher.py was checked and only asserts backpressure state; test_consumer.py was checked and covers only the happy path. A regression in the restart path (e.g. the new `if not process: continue` guard, the moved `self.process_restarts[process_index] += 1` increment after the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS comparison, or the isinstance-guarded kill leaving a zombie Thread alive while a new one is spawned) ships unverified; in production this code decides whether the whole consumer restarts, so a wrong branch means either infinite zombie respawn or spurious RuntimeError consumer crashes.

adjudication.rationale: The diff substantially rewrites the liveness/restart path in `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive` (per-process `process_healthy_since`, `process_restarts` dict, `is_alive()`/hang detection, `kill()` guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, and restarting via `_create_process_for_shards`). The updated/added tests only cover (a) the happy-path consumer behavior (`test_basic`) and (b) process-count/shard distribution (`test_flusher_processes_limit`), while `test_flusher.py` was only adjusted to check any backpressure value. Nothing in the diff exercises the unhealthy branches (dead process, hang timeout, restart counter threshold/RuntimeError, or thread-vs-process kill behavior), so a regression in these new critical branches would ship unverified.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The rewritten multi-process join() (per-process deadline slicing, terminate on each process) has no test — test_flusher.py and test_consumer.py in this diff both end with a bare step.join()/flusher join with no assertion that all processes terminated or that timeout semantics hold. The deadline arithmetic (`remaining_time <= 0: break` exits the whole for-loop, skipping terminate() for the remaining processes) is untested; if it's wrong, consumer shutdown leaves spawned flusher processes un-terminated and the consumer hangs on deploy/restart.

adjudication.rationale: In SpanFlusher.join(), when a timeout is provided, the loop does `remaining_time = deadline - time.time(); if remaining_time <= 0: break`, which exits the *entire* per-process loop and therefore skips the subsequent `process.terminate()` for any remaining processes (`for process_index, process in self.processes.items(): ... break ... if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.terminate()`). This can leave some spawned flusher processes running after join(timeout), a concrete shutdown/cleanup defect introduced by the multi-process join rewrite. The diff’s tests call `step.join()` but do not exercise/verify timeout semantics or that all processes are terminated, so this regression would go unnoticed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Default behavior silently changes from one flusher process total to one process per shard: with max_processes=None (the factory default when --flusher-processes is not passed), self.max_processes falls back to len(buffer.assigned_shards), spawning N processes each constructing its own SpansBuffer with its own Redis connections and Kafka producer. A consumer with e.g. 32 assigned shards goes from 1 flusher process to 32 on deploy with no config change, multiplying Redis connections and spawned processes by shard count; the CLI flag defaults to 1 only for the ingest-spans consumer, so any other construction path (or an operator omitting the flag) gets the shard-per-process explosion and potential resource exhaustion/COGS spike, with no backfill of the intended '1 process' behavior.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, the new `max_processes` defaults to `None` and is immediately converted via `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, which means the default behavior becomes `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` processes (and `_create_processes()` starts one per mapped shard-group). Previously the flusher created a single background process/thread (`_create_process()` with `self.buffer`). `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` also defaults `flusher_processes: int | None = None` and passes it through (`max_processes=self.flusher_processes`), so any construction path that doesn't explicitly set `flusher_processes` will now spawn one process per assigned shard. Although the ingest-spans click option defaults to 1, that default is only applied for that CLI wiring; the underlying default in the factory/flusher remains shard-count, making the behavior change real and silent for other call sites.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] submit() now calls record_stored_segments() on the flusher's fresh per-shard SpansBuffer instances (self.buffers) instead of the shared buffer the consumer's write path uses, so the original buffer passed to the flusher constructor never has record_stored_segments called on it in the parent process. If record_stored_segments carries any local/in-memory state on the buffer object (as opposed to a per-shard Redis write), the writer-side backpressure accounting that previously updated the shared buffer now updates orphaned copies, and backpressure detection silently degrades; anyone relying on the flusher honoring insertion-pause signals gets unbounded Redis growth instead.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that SpanFlusher no longer retains/uses the original `buffer` passed to `__init__` for `record_stored_segments()`: `self.buffer = buffer` was removed, per-process `SpansBuffer(shards)` instances are created in `_create_process_for_shards`, stored in `self.buffers`, and `submit()` now loops over `self.buffers.values()` calling `buffer.record_stored_segments()` instead. If any caller expected the *original* `SpansBuffer` object (potentially shared with the writer path) to have its in-memory accounting updated in the parent process, this change could break that expectation. However, the finding’s stronger claim about backpressure “silently degrading” into unbounded Redis growth cannot be verified from this diff alone because `SpansBuffer`’s internal behavior/state isn’t shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code — nothing in the diff or existing callers invokes it, and its behavior (restart by shard) is duplicated by the loop in _ensure_processes_alive calling _create_process_for_shards directly. The next person changing restart logic has two near-identical methods to reason about and may edit the dead one believing it runs; delete it.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `SpanFlusher` adds `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` but there is no call site shown for it within `flusher.py`; restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive` instead directly calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. `_create_process_for_shard` is therefore at least redundant with the primary restart path and may be unused, creating extra maintenance surface and potential confusion if someone updates restart behavior in one place but not the other. However, the claim that it has no callers anywhere in the repo cannot be fully verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Metric tags are inconsistent across the same code path: the produce/segment-size timers use tag key "shard" with a comma-joined list while wait_produce uses key "shards", so dashboards aggregating by shard tag split the same process's metrics into two cardinality streams. Anyone building flusher health dashboards per shard sees produce timings and wait_produce timings under different tag keys with different value formats (single int vs "0,2,3"), silently breaking aggregation.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.main`, the diff shows `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` and `metrics.timing("spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes", ..., tags={"shard": shard_tag})`, but `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})` uses a different tag key (`shards` vs `shard`) on the same code path. This will split otherwise-related metrics into different tag dimensions and can break shard-based aggregation in dashboards, but it does not affect runtime correctness of flushing itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The memory-pressure check in submit() now calls get_memory_info() on every per-shard-group SpansBuffer on every message, multiplying the remote/Redis memory-info calls by process count on the hot path. In the default configuration (max_processes=None -> one process per assigned shard), each consumed message now triggers N memory-info lookups instead of one; operators with many partitions see an N-fold increase in Redis round-trips and CPU on the consumer's submit path, degrading throughput exactly when the consumer is busiest.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.submit()`, the memory-pressure check changed from `list(self.buffer.get_memory_info())` to iterating all per-process buffers: `for buffer in self.buffers.values(): memory_infos.extend(buffer.get_memory_info())` (flusher.py). Since `self.buffers` is created per shard-group/process in `__init__`/`_create_process_for_shards` (each `SpansBuffer(shards)`), and the default `max_processes` becomes `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (i.e., one process per shard), this makes the submit-path call `get_memory_info()` N times per message instead of once. The diff supports the claimed N-fold increase in calls; it’s a throughput/performance concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In _ensure_processes_alive(), a crashed flusher process is kill()ed and replaced but never join()ed or waited on, so the killed SpawnProcess becomes a zombie until the replaced object is garbage-collected. Under a crash-looping flusher (e.g., Redis outage causing repeated exits), each restart cycle leaks a zombie process entry; the container accumulates zombies and can eventually hit the process limit, taking down the whole consumer even though the restart logic believes it is recovering.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher._ensure_processes_alive()` (new in this diff), when a per-shard flusher `multiprocessing.Process` is detected unhealthy, the code calls `process.kill()` (only for `multiprocessing.Process`) and immediately starts a replacement via `_create_process_for_shards(...)`, overwriting `self.processes[process_index]`. There is no corresponding `process.join()` / `wait()` anywhere in this restart path to reap the exited child. Since `kill()` does not wait for process termination, the old child can remain a zombie until reaped; with repeated restarts this can accumulate. The diff shows `join()`/reaping only in `SpanFlusher.join()` during shutdown, not during crash-loop restarts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] _create_process_for_shard() restarts a shard's process by creating a new one for the same process_index without killing or stopping the existing process first, so two processes would run concurrently for the same shards. Any future caller of this method (it is currently dead code — nothing in the diff invokes it) silently double-runs flushes for the same shards, producing duplicate Kafka production and racing on the shared backpressure/healthy Values; as written it is a latent trap for the next contributor who wires it up.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher`, `_create_process_for_shard()` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` which unconditionally creates and `start()`s a new process/thread and overwrites `self.processes[process_index]` without first terminating/killing the existing one for that `process_index` (contrast with `_ensure_processes_alive()`, which does try to `kill()` before recreating). That would indeed allow two concurrent workers for the same shard set *if this method were ever invoked*. However, nothing in the provided diff calls `_create_process_for_shard()` (and the main lifecycle uses `_ensure_processes_alive()`), so it’s a diff-grounded latent hazard rather than a currently verifiable behavior regression.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards) treats an explicitly configured value of 0 as falsy, silently falling back to one process per shard. An operator who sets --flusher-processes 0 intending to disable extra flusher processes gets the maximum process count instead, spawning one process per shard with no error or warning — the opposite of the requested configuration.

adjudication.rationale: In `SpanFlusher.__init__`, `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` will treat an explicitly passed `max_processes=0` as falsy and replace it with `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. Since the new CLI option `--flusher-processes` is `type=int` with no validation/min constraint, an operator can supply `0` and have it silently ignored, resulting in `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` spawning one process per shard—opposite of the configured value and without warning.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The produce and wait_produce timers use inconsistent tag keys ("shard" vs "shards") with a comma-joined shard-list value that changes on every partition rebalance or restart reassignment. Anyone building dashboards or alerts on spans.buffer.flusher.produce by shard gets two disjoint tag namespaces for the same logical dimension, and the comma-joined values churn as assignments change, fragmenting the metric series and making per-shard alerting unreliable.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows inconsistent metric tag keys for closely related timers: `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.produce", tags={"shard": shard_tag})` uses `shard`, while `metrics.timer("spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce", tags={"shards": shard_tag})` uses `shards` (in `SpanFlusher.main`). The value `shard_tag` is a comma-joined list of shards (`",".join(map(str, shards))`), which will change when shard assignments change, causing time series churn and making dashboards/alerts harder to build. This is a real, diff-grounded observability/design issue but not a functional correctness defect.
